opener.heading: Week 50: Animal Kingdom 🦉
about: Every animal Azlyn can name is out there in the middle of December doing one of three things: sleeping through it, gone south, or working all day to stay warm. She sorts them into those three groups on Friday. Then she feeds the ones who stayed, packs four bags of the right food for the ducks, and finds out from one hand in ice water why a seal gets by without a coat. Some animals sleep, some leave, some stay, and she tests that sentence against every creature in the house.

December does her one favor. The branches are bare, so the nests show, the hedges have nothing left to hide, and the mud by the gate freezes hard enough to hold a print for days. Friday's feeders hang by ten in the morning and every walk after that goes past them. On Wednesday she picks one animal and becomes the person in this house who knows the most about it, which is a bigger deal at three than it sounds.
azlyn: Who sleeps, who leaves, who stays. Three ways an animal gets through a winter, sorted into three trays with her own hands.
What a wild animal can eat and what it can't. Seed and oats and corn, and why bread fills a duck without feeding it.
Animal movement in her own body. Bear crawl, frog jump, snake, penguin, each one held for the length of a hallway.
Fat holds heat. One bare hand in ice water and one in a glove of shortening, and she calls the winner before you ask.
Reading evidence backwards. A print, a bitten apple, a tipped cup, and the story of what came through the kitchen in the night.
you: Outdoors helps even when nothing is happening
The day before is often better than the day itself
Performing for one attentive person is enough
Cabin fever is physiological, not attitudinal
Mid-December takes more than it gives, and the day should shrink
Being an expert on one thing is enormously motivating at three
A crater is a record of something that already happened, and reading it backwards is new thinking
shopping: Lard, suet or vegetable shortening, 2 cups (butter works for Tuesday)
Unsalted nuts, chopped, plus a handful still in their shells for Monday
Popcorn kernels and cranberries, fresh or dried (optional, for Friday's Try it)
A large blunt darning needle, adult hands only (for the Try it)
Blunt scissors, and your own sharp pair
A craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
Index cards, 11, or a cereal box to cut up
Thin card for the name tags and den signs
Large sheets of paper, 2, or the back of used wrapping paper
Plain drawing paper, a dozen sheets
Old magazines, catalogs or seed flyers, 2
Cardboard boxes, 3–4 to flatten (start saving now)
Parchment paper and a baking tray
A rolling pin and a table knife
A mixing bowl, plus one big enough to hold ice water
A small saucepan and a wooden spoon
3 shallow trays, baking sheets or box lids
Jar lids, 2, and 1 small jar with its lid
An old sock or a scrap of fabric
Washable non-toxic paint and a wide brush
A tote bag she can carry herself
An ice cube tray, filled the night before
A clock or a phone timer
Your phone, for one video and one recording
An animal book, whatever is already on the shelf
Every soft toy and toy animal in the house
Every coat and jacket by the front door
Sofa cushions, a blanket or sheet, and 2 dining chairs
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 18 months this week. He climbs the stairs holding the rail with a hand in yours, pretend play has started, and he has twenty-odd words and no volume control for any of them.

days.title: The Ones Who Didn't Leave
days.prepTonight: Stand the lard or shortening out of the fridge to soften, put the pinecones, the string and a saucepan beside it, and move a cup of frozen peas to the fridge for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: What They Can Eat and What They Can't

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: Feeding the Ones Who Didn't Leave

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Ten Still Minutes by the Feeder

opening.title: What They Can Eat and What They Can't
opening.need: 2 paper plates · 1 marker · a handful of birdseed · a handful of rolled oats · half an apple · 1 slice of bread.
steps: Write YES on one plate and NO on the other, big enough to read across the table.
Hand her the seed, the oats and the apple one at a time. Then the bread, which goes on NO: it fills a bird and feeds it nothing.
Ask what a small bird eats in December once the bugs are gone, then tell her you are fixing that at 9:15.

main.title: Feeding the Ones Who Didn't Leave
materials: 1 cup lard, suet or vegetable shortening (peanut butter works, check allergies first)
2 cups birdseed, or rolled oats plus sunflower seeds and chopped unsalted nuts
4–6 pinecones, or cardboard tubes and empty yogurt pots
1 ball of string, cut into arm-length pieces
1 small saucepan and a wooden spoon
1 apple, halved
1 small jar with a lid, for the afternoon's seed jar
Scissors (adult only)
2 paper plates and a spoon for the seed
steps: Tie string around each pinecone before anything gets sticky, a double knot under the top scales, and trim the ends. For pots and tubes, you make the holes and thread the string.
Melt the fat in the saucepan over a low burner until it runs clear, stir once with the wooden spoon and take it off the heat. She stays at the table for this.
Tip the seed onto one paper plate. You stir it into the pan off the heat until the spoon stands up on its own, then set it down to cool.
Once the pan is warm and no hotter, she presses the mix into the pinecone scales and packs the pots and tubes full.
Roll each loaded feeder in the spare seed on the second plate, tip what is left of it into a small jar with a lid for the afternoon, then twenty minutes in the fridge to set hard.
Hang them where you can both see them from a window and wedge the apple halves onto a twig alongside. She picks the tree.
main.tip: Hang one within a few feet of a bush. Chickadees will not cross open ground to a feeder with nowhere to bolt to.

outside.title: Ten Still Minutes by the Feeder
paras: Walk the block first and get the cold into her, then sit on the step under the feeders. Ten minutes of not moving. Nothing comes for the first five. Then a chickadee drops in and leaves with one seed, or a junco works the ground underneath. Whisper the tally: sparrows, a crow going over, the squirrel who found it first.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months with twenty-odd words. Give him a spare pinecone in the high chair while the fat is on the burner, and the carrying job once the pan is in the sink. He points at the window when something lands and says bird. On the step, sit him on your knee facing out for two still minutes rather than ten.

second.title: Sleeps, Leaves or Stays
second.intro: Three trays, three words, and every animal in the house lands in one of them by 2:30.
materials: 3 shallow trays, baking sheets or box lids
Every toy animal in the house
An old magazine, catalog or seed flyer for pictures
Blunt scissors and a glue stick
Paper and crayons for the drawings
1 marker for the three labels
steps: Trays in a row. Write SLEEPS, LEAVES and STAYS on three paper strips with the marker and let her set one in each tray.
Give her the three words in one sentence: some animals sleep underground until spring, some fly south, some stay right here.
Tip the toy animals out and let her sort. Leave the wrong ones where she puts them and ask where that animal would be tonight.
She cuts animals out of the magazine with the blunt scissors, glues them onto paper and adds them to a tray.
The ones with no toy and no picture, she draws: squirrel, frog, bear, deer, robin. You write each name beside the drawing.
Carry the STAYS tray to the window and hold it up beside the feeder. Everything in it is out there tonight in the dark.
second.tip: Robins split the tray: some go and some stay. Let her put one in each and leave it unsettled.

alternatives: Sort the toy animals by feet, then by teeth.
The STAYS tray only, and stop there.
Line every animal up along the hallway by size.
outAgain: Grandparents or a family visit, and she carries a spare feeder to hang in their yard
The park, looking up for nests in the bare trees on the way
A drive round the first streets with their lights up
The window seat and the bird book, if the wind has teeth in it

aroundWorld.title: Feeding the Birds at Midwinter 🐦
paras: In Norway and Sweden a julenek, a sheaf of oats on a pole, goes up in the yard before Christmas so the birds eat before the family does. In the United States the Christmas Bird Count has run every December since 1900, when a naturalist asked people to count birds instead of shooting them.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Thread popcorn and cranberries onto a short string, the blunt darning needle in adult hands only, and hang your own julenek outside on a branch, out of Kreston's reach and in view of the window. Pop a bowl for her at the same time and let her eat the difference.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Chickadees hide thousands of seeds every fall and grow extra brain tissue to remember where they put them.

days.krestonPM: He sorts too: one animal out of a tray, carried to another room. Give him three sturdy toys and a box lid. At 18 months he climbs stairs holding the rail with a hand in yours, so at the visit he will want them eleven times.

insight.headline: Outdoors helps even when nothing is happening.
paras: You take her out in weather nobody would choose, and half those walks produce nothing you could point to afterward. Ten still minutes on a step with no bird in sight is the part that pays. Her attention drifts and lands where it likes, which researchers who study green space call soft fascination, and it gives back the focus a morning of instructions burns through. Sitting rather than walking is what makes room for it. Kreston gets the same from your knee, facing out. A cold step and no birds is not a wasted three quarters of an hour, and you can stop apologizing for it.

days.safety: Melted fat scalds, and it holds that heat long after the pan stops looking dangerous, so she comes to it at step four and not before. Loose seed and chopped nuts are choking-size for Kreston at 18 months, so sweep the floor and his chair before you put him down. The hanging string goes out of reach the moment the feeders do. The sharp scissors stay with you; the blunt pair is hers this afternoon and comes back to you between cuts. Kreston is behind a gate or strapped into the high chair from the moment the pan goes on the burner until the pan is in the sink.

days.title: The Day Before the Ducks
days.prepTonight: Tip the thawed peas into a bowl, drain the corn, and stand the oats, the four paper bags and the marker on the table.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Every Animal Between Here and the Corner

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: A Home for a Pet We Don't Have

opening.title: Tearing the Lettuce
opening.need: half a head of lettuce · 1 mixing bowl · her washed hands.
steps: Bowl in front of her, lettuce leaves in a pile beside it. Tear the first one into pieces the size of her thumbnail and drop them in.
Hand her the rest. A duck has no teeth and swallows what it grabs, so anything bigger than a thumbnail gets torn again.
Ask who the bags are for. Four is the number in the book, and if she says six you can stretch the oats.

main.title: Four Bags for the Pond
materials: 2 cups rolled oats
1 cup frozen peas, thawed
1 cup canned or frozen corn, drained
Half a head of lettuce
4 paper bags or zip-top bags
1 marker and crayons
1 measuring cup
1 mixing bowl
steps: Stand the four bags open in a row, tops rolled down so they hold their shape.
She fills the measuring cup to the half-cup line with oats and tips one into each bag. Four bags, four fills, counted out loud.
A quarter cup of peas into each, then a quarter cup of corn, same cup, her hands. What lands on the table stays there until the end.
A fistful of torn lettuce on top of each one, straight from the bowl.
Labels: she draws the four foods on each bag with the crayons while you write the words underneath. Peas are green circles and that is close enough.
Roll the tops down and stand all four in the fridge by the door, so nobody hunts for them tomorrow.
main.tip: Bread is worth being firm about. It fills a duck without feeding it, and what sinks feeds the algae. Say it once today and she will say it to somebody at the pond tomorrow.

outside.title: Every Animal Between Here and the Corner
paras: Walk to the corner and back and count everything alive that is not a person. Dogs on leashes, a cat behind a storm door, crows working the gutter, house sparrows deep in a hedge, squirrels on the fence line. Keep the tally on her fingers and start again at ten. December has stripped the hedges, so she can see right into them.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months and pretend play has started, which today looks like him feeding a duck that is not in the room. Give him a paper bag with a fistful of torn lettuce and let him carry it up and down the kitchen. He empties it, you refill it. On the walk he points at every dog and names it before you do.

second.title: A Home for a Pet We Don't Have
second.intro: Azlyn has never owned a pet and has firm views about one. A shoebox holds all of them until the pet shop at 2:30.
materials: 1 shoebox with a lid
1 old sock or a scrap of fabric for the bedding
2 jar lids for food and water bowls
Card for a name tag, plus string
1 marker and crayons
Blunt scissors
Masking tape
One soft toy to move in
steps: She picks the pet first, and the box gets built around whichever soft toy she chooses.
Doorway next. She marks one end of the box with a crayon and cuts it out with the blunt scissors while you hold it steady.
Bedding: the sock or fabric folded flat into one end. Ask where a real one would sleep, by the door or the dark end.
Tape the two jar lids down inside for food and water so they cannot tip when she carries the box around, which she will.
Name tag: cut a rectangle of card, snip a nick in one corner with the blunt scissors, thread the string through it and tape the end to the front. She says the name, you write it.
On the lid she draws the care list: what it eats, how many times a day, who does it. Write her words underneath.
Move the pet in, lid half on. Tell her the box is coming to the pet shop.
second.tip: Take the box with you at 2:30 if she wants it. A three-year-old holding her own bowls against a shelf of real ones is doing the afternoon's thinking on the spot.

alternatives: Name every soft toy in the house and write the list.
Make a leash out of string and walk the pet round the downstairs.
Feed the pet a pretend dinner on the real plates.
outAgain: The pet shop, then the garden center next door for the tree stacks
The park, and count how many dogs get walked in an hour
A friend's house that has a cat, if anyone is home
Home early with the box and the animal books, if the rain has set in
days.krestonPM: Give him the shoebox lid and a soft toy of his own while the building goes on. At 18 months he tips things out and puts them back for as long as you leave him to it. In the pet shop the fish tanks hold him longer than anything with fur, and he has words for dog, cat and fish.

insight.headline: The day before is often better than the day itself.
paras: Azlyn will get more out of these four bags than out of the pond tomorrow, which is worth knowing before you skip a prep morning to save an hour. Wanting a thing and getting it run on different systems, and the wanting one fires harder and for longer: the reward signal climbs all through the run-up and levels off once the thing arrives. Preparing also hands her a job with a future attached, which she is new at. She holds tomorrow in her head all day. The pond takes nine minutes tomorrow and the bags took all morning, and both of those are the trip.

days.safety: The blunt scissors stay in her hand while you hold the box, and they come back to you between cuts. Cut the name-tag string short and put the offcut in the trash before you sit back down, because cord at Kreston's height is a strangling risk. The jar lids and the string leash from the alternatives go up out of his reach the moment she sets the box down.

days.title: The Show Kreston Watches
days.prepTonight: Pull two dining chairs into the living room, find a blanket big enough to hang across them, and cut a cereal box into eleven cards for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Nests You Can Only See in December

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Bath, Then the Recording One More Time

opening.title: Practicing the Entrances
opening.need: 1 sheet of paper · crayons · 1 wooden spoon.
steps: The morning builds an animal show for Kreston. Ask which four animals are in the show. Write the names down the page in crayon in her order and let her draw a small one beside each.
Practice one entrance each: how it walks on, the noise it makes, how it gets off again. Do them with her, and be terrible at it.
Hand her the wooden spoon and let her announce all four names into it. Tell her Kreston is the audience and the doors open at 9:15.

main.title: The Animal Show for Kreston
materials: Masking tape for the stage edge
1 blanket or sheet for the curtain
2 dining chairs to hang it from
1 cushion for Kreston
1 wooden spoon as the microphone
Paper and crayons for the running order
Your phone, to film one take
steps: Tape a rectangle on the floor. Inside that line is the stage.
Stand the two chairs behind it, back to back, and hang the blanket across them. She comes out from behind.
Cushion on the floor facing the stage. Kreston sits there, you sit beside him, and that is the whole audience.
Run the show. Each animal comes through the curtain, walks its walk, makes its noise into the wooden spoon, bows and goes back. She marks off each one in crayon as it finishes.
Film one take, start to finish, no stopping for the bits that go wrong.
Clap at the end. Then ask her to do the one Kreston liked best, again.
main.tip: Kreston will be on the stage before the second animal is done. Put him back on the cushion once, then let him stay in the show and let her direct him.

outside.title: The Nests You Can Only See in December
paras: Bare branches give you eight weeks a year when the nests show, so walk the street with your heads back. Small tight cups in the forks of hedges, a ragged ball of leaves high in an oak (a squirrel's, and it is called a drey), a gray paper wasp nest under a porch roof, nobody home. Count them out loud.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months and pretend play has arrived, so a sister being a bear lands for him now. He claps when Azlyn bows, copying applause before he understands it. On the walk, point up and wait: he follows a pointed finger to the thing at the end of it.

second.title: The Animal Radio Show
second.intro: Same four animals, same running order, no picture. Everything arrives through the ears this time.
materials: Your phone's voice recorder
1 cardboard tube as the microphone
Paper and crayons for the running order
A quiet room with the door shut
A cushion for Kreston to sit on for the playback
steps: Quiet room, door shut, everyone else out. Show her the record button and let her press it.
Test first: she says her own name into the cardboard tube while you hold the phone behind it, then play it back. She needs to hear herself once before anything else works.
New running order on paper. She draws the four animals again and can change the order.
Record the show. She announces each animal, then makes its noise, then moves to the next. Stay silent, so the recording is her voice on its own.
Bring Kreston in, sit him on the cushion and play it to him. Watch his face when his sister's voice comes out of your hand while she stands beside him.
Record take two if she wants one. She will, and she will fix things you did not point out.
Name the file and play it at dinner for Joseph, with her sitting there while it runs.
second.tip: Leave the mistakes in take one alone. She hears them on playback, close to the first time she has heard her own voice from outside her head.

alternatives: Sound effects only, and you guess the animal.
Record Kreston's noises and play them to him.
Puppet show from behind the sofa, no recording.
Two microphones, and she interviews you.
outAgain: Feeding the ducks, with yesterday's four bags out of the fridge
The park with the scooter, if the path is dry
A walk to see whose lights went up overnight
Home, the radio show on repeat, if the pond is iced or the wind is up
days.krestonPM: He comes to the pond in the carrier or with his hand in yours, and he gets a pinch of corn to drop from a step back. At 18 months he throws underarm and misses, so expect the corn to land at his feet and the ducks to come to him. Say duck every time. He has 20-plus words and this is a good one.

insight.headline: Performing for one attentive person is enough.
paras: Azlyn does not need a room of relatives, and a small audience gets you a better show. One person who watches the whole thing lets her run a sequence start to finish: four animals held in order, each one's move remembered, and a mistake survived without stopping. Kreston on his cushion is audience enough to make it real and not enough to make her self-conscious. He also wanders off partway, and a performer who keeps going once her audience has walked away has learned the other half of it. Save the big performance for people who ask for it. The one she puts on for her brother is the one she rehearses.

days.safety: December water is cold enough to matter within minutes and the pond bank is slick underfoot, so both children stay off it. Azlyn throws her handful from a step back with you standing beside her, and Kreston stays in the carrier or holds a hand the whole time you are near the water.

days.title: The Way Animals Move
days.prepTonight: Eleven cards cut and stacked on the table with the crayons, and the hallway cleared end to end so there is a run at it.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Warm Bath After a Big Day

opening.title: The Animal Deck
opening.need: 11 index cards or a cut-up cereal box · crayons · 1 marker.
steps: Ten animals, one per card. She names them and draws them, you write the word underneath with the marker.
Try each one at the table as it gets drawn: bear on all fours, frog from a squat, snake on her belly, penguin with her feet together.
Shuffle the ten and stack them face down. Nobody turns one over until 9:15.

main.title: Bear Crawl to the Kitchen
materials: 11 index cards or a cut-up cereal box
Crayons and 1 marker
Masking tape to mark the stations
4–6 sofa cushions
1 dining chair to go under
1 soft ball to carry between her knees
steps: Tape five crosses on the floor: front door, hallway, doorway, living room, kitchen. The gaps between them are the course.
Lay the cushions across one gap as stepping stones, stand the dining chair over another so she has to go under it, and leave the ball at station four.
She turns the top card. That animal is how she travels to the next cross, and no other way counts.
Card by card, all the way to the kitchen. The ball goes between her knees for the penguin stretch and she waddles it there.
Shuffle and run it backward, you doing the same animal wrong enough that she has to correct you.
Let her draw an eleventh card: an animal she invents, with a move nobody has done. It goes on top of the deck.
main.tip: She will want the deck again tomorrow. Leave it stacked by the door and let her run the course on her own, without the tape and without you.

outside.title: Hiding Nuts Like a Squirrel
paras: Take a handful of unshelled nuts to the park and let her hide them the way gray squirrels do, one at a time, under leaf litter or in the crook of a root. Ten hiding places, no two together. Walk away, come back and find them. She loses two. Squirrels lose most of theirs, and the ones they forget come up as oak trees.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months and carries things while he walks, which is newer than it looks. The nuts stay in Azlyn's bag, so give him a wide pine cone to hold on the way and let him put it wherever he decides. On the course at home, tape a station of his own at the low end. He follows Azlyn along the cushions and gets up to do it again.

second.title: Moving the Whole Herd Upstairs
second.intro: Every soft toy in the house is moving to a new home on the landing, and she carries every one of them there.
materials: Every soft toy in the house
1 laundry basket
1 blanket for the river
3–4 cushions for the crossing
1 tote bag she can carry herself
Masking tape to mark the new home
steps: Tape a square on the landing carpet. That is the new home, and everything ends up inside it.
Pile every soft toy at the bottom of the stairs, counted out loud as they land.
Spread the blanket across the hall floor and lay the cushions on it as stones. Anything crossing the river crosses on the stones.
She ferries them over the river in the laundry basket, a load at a time, dragging it. Anything that falls in is lost and gets rescued from the far bank.
At the foot of the stairs the basket stops. Toys go into the tote bag over her shoulder, one hand on the rail, and up she goes.
Trips until the pile is gone. You carry the basket up at the end with the leftovers.
She arranges the herd inside the taped square and decides who sleeps next to who. It stays there overnight.
second.tip: Do not speed this up. The slow, heavy, repeated trip is the whole afternoon, and a child allowed to do it fifteen times comes down the other side settled.

alternatives: The river only, crossed on cushions, no move.
Move the herd to one room downstairs instead.
Sort them into big, medium and small before anyone travels.
Put the whole herd in the basket and pull it round like a train.
outAgain: The neighborhood park, and she gets to the top of the climbing frame her own way
A walk with the scooter, if the sidewalks are dry
The woods path, to see how the animal moves work on uneven ground
Indoor playground, if the rain is horizontal
days.krestonPM: Give him the empty laundry basket in the hall and let him push it. At 18 months a basket to lean on is a walker with a purpose, and he will run it into every wall in the house. Keep him off the stairs while Azlyn works them, with two toys of his own to carry at the bottom.

insight.headline: Cabin fever is physiological, not attitudinal.
paras: By the third indoor day in December Azlyn is climbing the back of the sofa and shouting at nothing, and the read on that is a body with a need it cannot name. Her vestibular and proprioceptive systems, the ones that track where she is and how hard she is pushing, get their input from spinning, hanging, crawling and carrying. Winter cuts that supply off. The result looks like defiance and reads as hunger. A morning of bear crawls and hauled baskets feeds it, and you get the child back at lunch without a single conversation about behavior. Fifteen minutes of hard work through her arms and legs beats an hour of asking her to settle.

days.safety: Nuts in their shells are the worst choking size there is at 18 months, and today puts ten of them at ground level. They stay in Azlyn's bag until the moment she buries each one, and you check the ground where she was digging before Kreston walks it. Stairs with her hands full. She goes up empty-handed or with the bag on her shoulder, never with the loaded basket, and the stair gate goes across behind her if you have one, because Kreston climbs stairs holding on now and will follow her up the second you turn around. With no gate, he stays at the bottom with you and two toys of his own.

days.title: How Animals Stay Warm
days.prepTonight: Fill the ice cube tray and stand the tub of shortening on the counter, then leave every coat in the house piled by the front door.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The One-Glove Walk to the Gate

opening.title: Warmest Coat in the House
opening.need: every coat and jacket by the front door · her two hands.
steps: Spread them out and let her put three on, one over the other, and walk around like that.
Hands inside each one. Thick and puffy, thin and slippery, fleece, wool. She ranks them warmest to coldest and you take her order as final.
Ask what a duck on the pond wears, since it has no coat and no closet. Feathers gets you halfway, and the other half is at 9:15.

main.title: The Glove Made of Butter
materials: 2 zip-top freezer bags
1 cup vegetable shortening, lard or butter
1 large mixing bowl
Ice cubes and cold water
1 spoon for packing the fat
A dish towel to dry hands
A clock or phone timer
steps: Fill the bowl half full of cold water, tip the ice in and leave it two minutes while you build the glove. Dish towel beside it, flat.
She spoons the cup of shortening into one bag and pushes it into the corners with the back of the spoon. The second bag stays empty.
Bare bag first. Her hand goes into the empty one and into the water. Count to twenty out loud and let her pull out whenever she wants.
Now the fat bag. Hand in, fat squeezed around it, into the water, same count. She will tell you the difference before you ask.
Both hands in together for the last test, one minute on the timer, and she calls which one she would keep. Hands out when she says, onto the dry towel.
Ask which animals wear that layer under their skin. Seals, whales, walruses, polar bears, all of them warm where she has a coat.
main.tip: Bare hand first. Run the fat glove first and she has nothing to measure it against, and the hour turns into playing with lard.

outside.title: The One-Glove Walk to the Gate
paras: One glove on, one hand bare, and walk to the gate and back reporting on both. It takes about ninety seconds for the difference to arrive, and she will start shaking the bare hand without noticing. Glove back on at the gate, then do the walk you planned with both hands covered.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months, and 18-month-old hands go cold fast and get complained about late. He pulls mittens off as a game, so use the pair on a string through his sleeves and check his fingers at the gate. Let him touch the surface of the water at home, once, with you holding his wrist and the towel open.

second.title: The Sofa Zoo
second.intro: The sofa comes apart this afternoon and goes back together as a row of dens, one per animal in the house.
materials: All the sofa cushions
8–10 towels and dish towels
Heavy books, 3–4, to weight the roofs
Every soft toy
1 laundry basket as the biggest den
1 flashlight
Masking tape and card for the name signs
Blunt scissors
1 marker
steps: Strip the sofa. Cushions on the floor in a long row on their edges, and the gaps between them are the dens.
Roof each den with a towel, weighted with a book or tucked into the gap. The laundry basket goes upside down over the far end for the biggest animal.
Every den gets its animal, and the animal has to fit. A bear in a dish towel den is a discovery she makes herself.
Line each one with a dish towel so nobody sleeps on a bare floor.
Signs: cut card into strips, she says the name, you write it with the marker, she tapes it to the front.
Big light off, flashlight on, and she gives you the tour, one animal at a time, while you ask the questions.
The zoo stays standing until dinner, and she goes back into it at 4:15 with the flashlight.
second.tip: Let her get inside the biggest den. She has spent the afternoon building warm dark spaces and she wants one of her own.

alternatives: One den, one animal, under the dining table.
Wrap every animal in a dish towel and line them up.
Sort the animals into who needs a warm den and who does not.
outAgain: Swimming, and warm water on a cold day is the whole argument
Indoor playground, if the pool is booked out by school parties
The library, for a book about seals and one about the Arctic
Home in the warm with the zoo, if two children into a pool is one thing too many
days.krestonPM: He walks the shallow end holding one of your hands and lets go before you are ready. Twenty-five minutes is the December ceiling, and he goes into the towel the moment his lips change. At 18 months the getting-dressed fight runs longer than the swim, so lay his clothes out in order before you get in.

insight.headline: Mid-December takes more than it gives, and the day should shrink.
paras: Three things land on the same two weeks: the light is gone by five, somebody has a cold that has been passed around twice, and the calendar is full of other people's plans. None of that is a failure of will. Your energy sets the ceiling for the day, and there is no version where you push through it for free. Cut the day down to fit: one activity instead of two, the same book twice, an afternoon of cushions on the floor. Azlyn reads the day off your face rather than off the schedule, and a calm adult doing less beats a frayed one doing all of it.

days.safety: No single dip in the ice water runs past a minute, and the bare hand goes in twice at most. Hands come out when she says so and go straight onto a dry towel. Kreston touches the surface for a second or two, no immersion, and onto the towel from there. The glove goes back on at the gate before the walk starts, and if it is below freezing the bare-hand test happens on the doorstep instead. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: Her One Animal
days.prepTonight: Flatten three or four boxes and stand them behind the sofa, put the big sheet of paper and the tape measure out, and check you have flour and salt in for tomorrow.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Where Her Animal Would Live Around Here

opening.title: The Shortlist of Three
opening.need: 1 large sheet of paper · crayons · 1 marker.
steps: Ask for three animals she would want to know everything about. Write the names across the top of the paper with the marker, spaced out.
One question each, out loud: what does it eat? She will know one, guess one and invent one, and all three tell you something.
She picks one and circles it. The other two get crossed out by her hand, not yours.

main.title: The Expert Wall
materials: 1 large sheet of paper, a flattened box, or the back of used wrapping paper
Crayons and 1 marker
Masking tape
An old magazine or catalog for pictures
Blunt scissors and a glue stick
Any animal book already in the house
steps: Tape the sheet to the wall low enough for her to reach the bottom.
Write her animal's name across the top with the marker, then rule four bands down the sheet: EATS, SLEEPS, MOVES, SAYS.
Take the bands one at a time. She draws in each with the crayons and you write her answer beside it word for word, wrong ones included.
The ones she cannot answer, look up in the animal book and add underneath. Two facts from a book is plenty for one wall.
She cuts pictures out of the magazine with the blunt scissors and glues them where she wants. A dog standing in for a wolf is a good decision.
Leave the bottom strip blank. She fills it at 4:15, and the wall stays up.
main.tip: Write what she says. He sleeps in a hole he dug hisself is worth more on that wall than a tidy sentence you supplied.

outside.title: Where Her Animal Would Live Around Here
paras: Take her animal out with you and find it somewhere to live on your own street. Under the deck, in the hollow at the base of the big tree, along the ditch behind the fence, up in the ivy. December strips the cover back, so she can see into places hidden in June. Ask what it would eat here, and let the answer be trash cans.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months and points at pictures in books and waits for you to name them, the work Azlyn is doing on the wall. Hold him up to the finished sheet and name two things on it. Give him his own crayon and the corner of a flattened box on the floor, and expect the scribble to leave the box.

second.title: Her Animal, Actual Size
second.intro: Her animal might be five feet long, and that number means nothing to her until it is lying on the hallway floor.
materials: 3–4 flattened cardboard boxes
1 craft knife or heavy scissors (adult only)
Packing tape and masking tape
1 tape measure or a length of string
Crayons, or washable non-toxic paint and a wide brush
Newspaper to work on
1 marker
The animal book from this morning
Your phone, for the length and one photo
steps: Find the real length in the animal book or on your phone, measure it along the hall floor and mark both ends with masking tape. She walks it heel to toe.
Newspaper down the hall. Lay the flattened boxes end to end between the marks and join them with packing tape.
Draw the outline. You hold the marker, she says where the head goes, how long the tail is, where the legs come out. Follow her even when the legs are wrong.
Cut it out with the craft knife or the heavy scissors while she stands back at the far mark, and tell her why.
She colors it in with the crayons, or paints it with the wide brush if you can face that, on her knees on the newspaper.
Write the name and the length across its side with the marker: WOLF, 5 FEET.
Tape it to the hallway wall and stand her beside it. Photograph the two of them.
second.tip: Do not correct the proportions. A tail out of the wrong end still teaches her the animal is longer than the hall is wide.

alternatives: Draw round Azlyn on a flattened box instead and cut her out.
Measure her animal in Azlyns, laid end to end.
Make a small paper version and stick it on the expert wall.
outAgain: Indoor playground, and a warm hour where nobody has to hold a marker
The library, if her animal needs a book you do not own
The park, to see whether the drey she found on Sunday is still up there
A drive to the pet store to look at something alive
days.krestonPM: At indoor playground he goes up the toddler steps and down the slide on his front, and at 18 months he runs that loop for ten or fifteen minutes, wanders off, then comes back to it twice more before you leave. Stay in the little-kid section. Back home, lie the cardboard animal on the floor and let him walk the length of it.

insight.headline: Being an expert on one thing is enormously motivating at three.
paras: Azlyn knowing more about wolves than anyone else in the house changes how she works. A child with one deep interest holds longer attention, asks harder questions and takes in vocabulary that would bounce off her in any other context: den, prey, pack, howl, all learned in an afternoon because they attach to something she has chosen. Researchers who follow these interests find they run for months and carry gains in knowledge and persistence. The subject matters less than the depth. Feed the one she picks, even when it is the fourth week of wolves, and let her be the one who knows.

days.safety: The craft knife is adult-only and goes back on a high shelf between cuts, not the arm of the sofa. Cut the cardboard on the floor with her standing back, and check the offcuts for staples before Kreston is put down anywhere near them.

days.title: Who Was Here
days.prepTonight: After she is asleep, lay the scene on the kitchen floor: a trail of flour prints, the bitten apple, a scatter of seed, the cup on its side, a tuft of cotton by the door. Cut the potato stamp and hide it.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Real Prints in the Frozen Mud

opening.title: Whose Foot Made That
opening.need: the trail, left where it is · 1 flashlight · paper and 1 marker.
steps: The flour trail you laid last night waits on the kitchen floor. Let her find it. Say nothing and follow with the flashlight; it is still dark at eight.
Kneel at one clear print and count the toes, then put her hand beside it for the size.
Write her first guess at the top of the paper. Nobody checks it until 9:15.

main.title: Something Came in the Night
materials: Half a cup of flour for the prints
1 potato and a table knife to cut the paw stamp (adult only)
1 apple with a bite out of it
A handful of sunflower seeds
1 plastic cup, tipped over
1 cotton ball pulled into a tuft of fur
Paper, a marker, and sticky notes to number the clues
1 flashlight
steps: Walk the scene together and put a numbered sticky note by each thing out of place: prints, apple, seeds, tipped cup, tuft of fur.
Take them in order. Ask what each tells her and write the answer under its number. Seeds on the floor mean it could reach. A bitten apple means teeth.
Follow the flour trail with the flashlight, walking the way the toes point, and ask which end it came in at.
Hand her the potato stamp and let her print a row of paws beside the trail. She works out that the stamp made the others.
Ask her to tell it from the beginning: how it got in, what it did, where it went. Write it word for word and read it back.
Let her lay a fresh trail across the hall after Kreston is in bed, for Joseph to find tonight.
main.tip: Do not confess. She will ask whether you did it, and what do you think? keeps the morning alive another twenty minutes.

outside.title: Real Prints in the Frozen Mud
paras: Frozen ground holds a print for days, so the mud by the gate and the strip under a fence are worth kneeling in front of. Dog prints everywhere, cat prints in the flower bed, bird prints like forks by standing water. She brings home one stick and one leaf for this afternoon.

days.infant: Kreston is 18 months and pretend play has begun, so he follows Azlyn along the trail doing his version of whatever she does. Put his hand flat in the flour and lift it straight up, then show him the print. He does it with two hands as long as the floor stays floured.

second.title: The Prints That Keep
second.intro: The flour trail comes off the floor before lunch. These go in the oven and come out hard enough to hang up.
materials: 2 cups flour, 1 cup salt, 1 cup water
1 mixing bowl
1 rolling pin
1 baking tray and parchment paper
1 cup or jar lid to cut rounds
Toy animals with molded feet
1 stick and 1 leaf from the morning walk
1 drinking straw for the hanging holes
String, cut into short lengths
steps: Flour and salt into the bowl, water last. She mixes with her hands until it comes together, five minutes of kneading and the calmest part of the day.
Roll it out to a finger's thickness with the rolling pin. Thin ones snap in the oven.
Cut rounds with the cup or the jar lid and lay them on the parchment-lined tray, not touching.
Press one thing into each round: a toy animal's foot, the end of the stick, the leaf laid flat and peeled off, her own thumb.
Punch a hole near the edge of every round with the drinking straw, off center so they hang straight.
Nothing bakes in an empty house, so the tray waits on the counter while you are out. Oven on its lowest setting when you get home at 3:30, tray in, timer set for two hours.
They come out at 5:30 and cool overnight on a windowsill. She threads a short length of string through each hole at breakfast and picks who gets which.
second.tip: Make four more than you need. Two crack in the oven, one warps, and the spare is the one she gives away.

alternatives: Press the prints into play dough and skip the oven.
Paint the toy animals' feet and stamp them onto paper.
Make one big round with everybody's thumb in it and date it.
outAgain: The hardware store, for a hook to hang the salt dough prints on
The park, to check the frozen mud by the gate again
A walk past Friday's feeders to see what is left of them
The grocery store, and she carries the list
days.krestonPM: The hardware store is a good hour for him: wide aisles, nothing precious at his height, and at 18 months he names half of what he sees at a volume you cannot do anything about. Let him carry the hook in its packet. Keep the salt dough out of his hands, cooled or not.

insight.headline: A crater is a record of something that already happened, and reading it backwards is new thinking.
paras: A print in flour, a bitten apple, a cup on its side: all of it is left over from the event. Azlyn spent the morning working from what is here now back to what must have happened, the move a geologist makes at a crater and a doctor makes with a rash. Three-year-olds can do this and seldom get asked to. Give her the evidence and she builds the story herself, and her questions on the way (which direction, how big, what next) are the method. The same move works on an empty plate and a wet footprint by the bath.

days.safety: Salt dough is dangerous if eaten and seriously so for an 18-month-old and for any dog in the house. Count the rounds in and out and store them high. The oven is on for two hours, so say it out loud each time she comes near. Keep the flour to the one stretch of kitchen floor you can see across, stay beside Kreston every second he is printing on it, and sweep it up the moment the story is told, because a floured floor is slick under new walkers. The hall trail goes down after Kreston is in bed and comes up before he is out of his room in the morning, so he never walks on it. The sunflower seeds and the cotton tuft go off the floor and into your pocket the moment their sticky notes are read, because both are choking size at 18 months and he is down there on the trail with her.
